Argentina’s Major Banks Hit by Targeted Foreign Sanctions, Industry Faces Disruption

BUENOS AIRES, June 14 — Argentina’s banking industry was thrown into turmoil this week after a coalition of foreign governments imposed sanctions on several of the country’s largest financial firms, freezing assets held abroad and restricting their access to international payment networks. The measures, which took effect late Tuesday, have already had sweeping effects across the sector, with numerous bank branches reporting operational disruptions and growing uncertainty among staff.

The sanctions target a group of prominent Argentine banks, including Banco del Plata, Andina Bank, and Rio Sur Bancorp, as well as their subsidiaries in neighboring countries. Industry sources said that overseas accounts belonging to these institutions have been blocked, while correspondent banking relationships with major international partners were abruptly suspended.

“We are facing a very serious situation. Our access to foreign currency and certain payment systems has been cut off,” said Silvia Marcón, spokesperson for the Argentine Banking Association. “Staff in international divisions have been instructed to halt cross-border transactions, and many teams are working overtime to assess the legal and operational implications.”

Workers at affected banks reported confusion and mounting concerns over job security. “We’ve had emergency meetings all week,” said Javier Lucero, a mid-level manager at Andina Bank. “Many employees are worried about possible layoffs if the situation drags on, especially in departments handling foreign transfers and compliance.”

As of Friday, at least 240 bank branches in Buenos Aires and provincial capitals reported curtailed operations, with customers unable to complete certain international transactions. At Banco del Plata’s central office, security personnel were seen restricting entry to employees not directly involved in crisis response teams.

Union representatives said they are monitoring the evolving situation closely. “Our priority is protecting jobs, and we are demanding transparency from management about the bank’s plans,” said Claudia Funes, secretary general of the National Bank Workers’ Federation.

Analysts warn that the longer the sanctions remain in effect, the greater the risk to the industry’s stability. “The Argentine banking sector is highly interconnected with global finance. Prolonged isolation could lead to liquidity problems and operational bottlenecks,” said Martín Esquivel, a financial consultant in Buenos Aires.

The Central Bank of Argentina issued a brief statement late Thursday, urging calm and stating that it is “working with the affected institutions to ensure the continued functioning of domestic operations.” However, the regulator acknowledged “significant challenges” in maintaining normal services at branches and processing centers directly impacted by the sanctions.

Negotiations between Argentine authorities and the governments behind the sanctions are reportedly ongoing, but officials gave no timeline for a possible resolution.
